summary: Kathryn Grayson Nanz opens by introducing her background bridging design and development, noting that AI introduces unique UX challenges due to its non-deterministic nature and entirely new interaction patterns. While developers live and breathe concepts like prompt engineering, hallucinations, and RAG, most users remain unfamiliar with these ideas, creating one of the widest knowledge gaps she has seen with any technology. AI currently has a serious UX problem: users see AI added everywhere but often encounter poorly designed features they barely understand, leading to frustration and eventual disengagement after repeated sub-par results. She draws an extended metaphor to the Macintosh GUI introduction, which succeeded by meeting users where they were—borrowing real-life vocabulary, using literal icons, and walking users through new concepts. Over time, as users became more literate, the UI evolved. She places AI currently at roughly "system 3" in this metaphor—not starting from scratch, but unable to assume expertise. She examines AI chat interfaces as borrowing familiar patterns from direct messaging while needing adaptation for AI-specific needs. She explains why AI cannot yet design these interfaces: AI can only remix existing patterns, and standardized AI UI patterns do not yet exist. She frames the solution around five user challenge categories: trust, clarity, control, transparency, and meaningful benefit. For trust, she advocates honesty about limitations and building patterns that empower users to verify outputs through citations, action plans for agentic workflows, and clear AI content labeling. For clarity, she critiques the "magic" framing of AI, advocating streaming text, chain-of-thought visibility, and highlighting new or changed content. For control, she emphasizes emergency brakes, safe exploration via version history and undo mechanisms, and granular control enabling users to keep some output aspects while reverting others—especially important as token costs rise. For transparency, she stresses users need to see what AI can access, what actions it takes, permissions granted (not just binary but granular), data retention with the ability to forget, cost/time estimates, and visual signals when AI acts independently like browser control. For meaningful benefit, she warns against assuming users know how to use AI, recommending examples, templates, suggested prompts, guided workflows, next-step action buttons, and direct integrations with other tools. She concludes that as models improve, the differentiator for AI-powered software is no longer performance but the quality of experiences built around them, and the line between design and development is blurring—developers must now consider trust, control, and transparency regardless of title.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: AI has a serious UX problem: users are overwhelmed with poorly designed AI features they barely understand, leading to frustration and disengagement after repeated sub-par results.
The knowledge gap between developers and users regarding AI is one of the widest seen with any technology, making UX crucial for bridging what developers intend and what users experience.
Five user challenge categories for AI—trust, clarity, control, transparency, and meaningful benefit—each must be addressed to help users get full value from AI.
Trust requires citations linking to source material, action plans shown before agentic workflows execute, and clear labeling of AI-generated content to avoid users feeling deceived.
Clarity means avoiding the "magic" framing of AI; streaming text, chain-of-thought visibility, and highlighting new content keep users engaged and enable accurate revisions.
Control demands clear emergency brakes, safe exploration through version history and undo mechanisms, and granular control letting users keep some output aspects while reverting others.

Transparency requires users to see what AI accesses, granular permissions beyond binary yes/no, data retention with the ability to forget, cost/time estimates, and visual signals when AI acts independently.
Meaningful benefit means never assuming users know how to use AI—provide examples, templates, suggested prompts, guided workflows, next-step action buttons, and direct tool integrations.
As AI models improve, the differentiator for AI-powered software is no longer performance but the quality of experiences built around them.
The line between design and development is blurring—developers must now consider trust, control, transparency, and user experience regardless of title.

sections.title: Introduction and AI's UX Problem
sections.summary: Kat introduces her background bridging design and development. She explains AI's non-deterministic nature and new interaction patterns create a wide knowledge gap between developers and users. AI has a serious UX problem: poorly designed features lead to user frustration and disengagement, and developers have limited chances to get it right.

sections.title: Macintosh GUI Metaphor
sections.summary: She draws an extended metaphor to the Macintosh GUI introduction, which succeeded by meeting users where they were with familiar vocabulary, literal icons, and guided onboarding. Over time, as user literacy grew, the UI became more technical. She places AI at roughly "system 3"—not starting from scratch but unable to assume expertise.

sections.title: Adapting Chat Interface Patterns for AI
sections.summary: She examines AI chat interfaces as an example of borrowing familiar patterns from direct messaging while needing adaptation for AI-specific features like reference sources, stopping in-progress replies, and agentic tools. She compares Copilot research agent chat with Teams chat to show how agent UIs lower barriers to entry.

sections.title: Why Not AI-Designed Interfaces
sections.summary: She addresses why AI cannot yet design AI interfaces: AI can only remix existing patterns, and standardized AI UI patterns do not fully exist yet. AI-generated UI looks average—fine as a starting point but insufficient for novel interaction modes requiring more UX attention, not less.

sections.title: Five User Challenges Framework
sections.summary: She introduces five categories of user challenges with AI—trust, clarity, control, transparency, and meaningful benefit—and explains that addressing each will help create AI experiences that support users through the introduction of this new technology.

sections.title: Trust: The Biggest Hurdle
sections.summary: She dives into trust as the number one hurdle. Users see AI as a black box, and hallucinations persist even as models improve. Rather than claiming your AI is more trustworthy, she advocates honesty about limitations and building patterns that empower users to verify and correct outputs—"trust, but verify."

sections.title: Trust: Citations, Agentic Workflows, and AI Content Labeling
sections.summary: She explains citations serve dual purposes: letting users validate AI output and repurpose material with a trail of accuracy. Implementation options include tooltips, inline links, and side panel reference windows. For agentic workflows, she stresses showing action plans for user approval before execution. She also addresses AI-generated content skepticism, recommending clear labeling—watermarks, disclaimers, asterisks—to avoid users feeling deceived.

sections.title: Clarity: Streaming, Chain of Thought, and Highlighting
sections.summary: She critiques the "magic" framing of AI, including the sparkle icon, advocating instead for clarity over dramatics. Streaming text disguises latency while keeping users actively engaged and able to assess output immediately. Having AI think out loud via chain-of-thought visibility improves confidence and enables more accurate revisions. Highlighting new or changed content helps users track autonomous AI actions.

sections.title: Control: Emergency Brakes and Safe Exploration
sections.summary: She emphasizes users must remain in control, able to stop or override AI at any point with a clear, prominent emergency brake. Drawing on Nielsen's safe exploration heuristic, she argues version history is now non-negotiable for non-deterministic output, with complexity scaling by task—from simple rephrasing for basic chat, to undo/redo for ~10 steps in document editing, to checkpoints and save states for advanced work. Granular control lets users keep some output aspects while reverting others, especially important as token costs rise.

sections.title: Transparency: Permissions, Data, Costs, and Autonomous Signals
sections.summary: She covers transparency in depth: users must see what AI tools access and how. Permissions are not binary—agents might read data vs. delete tables, read emails vs. send from them—and should support gray zones like temporary approvals, scoped access, and notifications. Systems that remember must also forget, with users having final say. Users need cost and time estimates before approving actions. Visual signals like banners or outlines must indicate when AI acts independently, such as taking browser control.

sections.title: Meaningful Benefit: Guided Workflows and Integrations
sections.summary: She warns against assuming users know how to use AI. Rather than presenting a blank text box, provide examples, templates, suggested prompts, and guided workflows demonstrating success. Next-step action buttons help users leverage output immediately—sharing, printing, posting. Direct integrations with other tools (word processors, code repos, ticketing systems) make AI part of daily workflow rather than a novelty.

sections.title: Conclusion: Experience Is the Differentiator
sections.summary: She concludes that as models improve, performance is no longer the differentiator—experience quality is. The line between design and development is blurring; developers must consider trust, control, and transparency regardless of title. Users must remain at the center of everything built for AI to be truly successful.
